L01.subgoal: Identify the core concepts, terms, and learning objectives of the XR course

key_points.text: The course introduces four related terms: Virtual Reality (VR), Augmented Reality (AR), Extended Reality (XR), and Mixed Reality (MR).
A primary focus of the course is determining the definitions and differences between these multiple terms and technologies.
The course aims to address the significance of these technologies and their relevance to the learner's future prospects.
Finding answers to these fundamental questions is stated as one of the main objectives of the course.

key_terms.definition: XR stands for extended reality.
VR stands for virtual reality.
AR stands for augmented reality.
MR is another term called mixed reality.

L01.subgoal: Identify the diverse applications and scope of AR, VR, and XR technologies

key_points.text: The common perception of AR, VR, and XR often involves fantastic, magical, or imaginary scenes from movies or video games.
The most common perception of Virtual Reality (VR) is that a user wears a headset that blocks vision and transports them to a virtual world.
Augmented Reality (AR) can involve seeing virtual objects overlaid onto the real world, such as in games like Pokemon Go.
XR technologies can be used for non-entertainment purposes, such as viewing extinct species or visualizing internal biological structures.

key_terms.definition: It is worn on the head, blocks our vision, and transports us to a virtual world which we can experience through the headset.

L01.subgoal: Explain how XR functions as an umbrella term for all immersive technologies

key_points.text: XR (Extended Reality) is an umbrella term that encapsulates all other related technologies, including AR, VR, and MR.
XR refers to all present or future immersive technologies.
The term 'X' in XR can refer to a variable that represents specific technologies like Augmented (A), Virtual (V), or Mixed (M) Reality.
An immersive experience is one perceived through sensory organs where the environment is indistinguishable from our real environment.

key_terms.definition: XR is an umbrella term that encapsulates all present or future immersive technologies, including AR, VR, and MR.
These are technologies where the user experiences an environment through sensory organs in a way that makes them fail to distinguish it from reality.
It describes a perceived experience through sensory organs that appears to be real, causing the user to assume the environment is real.
AR is one of the specific technologies that falls under the umbrella of Extended Reality (XR).
VR is one of the specific technologies that falls under the umbrella of Extended Reality (XR).
MR is one of the specific technologies that falls under the umbrella of Extended Reality (XR).

L01.subgoal: Define and differentiate the concepts of Augmented Reality, Augmented Virtuality, and Mixed Reality

key_points.text: The reality-virtuality continuum is a scale ranging from the real environment (nothing virtual) to the virtual environment (nothing real).
Augmented Reality (AR) involves augmenting the real world with digital or virtual content.
Augmented Virtuality (AV) involves augmenting the virtual world with real-world content.
The entire space between the real and virtual extremes is broadly referred to as Mixed Reality.

key_terms.definition: It is essentially referring to a scale that spans from the real environment to the virtual environment.
This is one extreme of the scale where there is nothing virtual.
This is the other extreme of the scale where there is nothing real.
In augmented reality, we are augmenting the real world with virtual content.
Augmented virtuality is the opposite of augmented reality, where we are augmenting the virtual world with real world content.
Mixed reality is the entire space between the virtual environment and the real environment.

L01.subgoal: Summarize core XR concepts and understand the course objectives and scope

key_points.text: XR refers to extended reality, which involves augmenting or replacing our perception of reality using systems.
The course will use a virtual reality system related to digital heritage preservation as its primary example.
Learning XR concepts is important because these fields are major emerging technologies required by industry and academia.
The reality-virtuality continuum was referenced from the 1994 paper, 'A Taxonomy of Mixed Reality Visual Displays,' by Paul Milgram and Fumio Kishino.

key_terms.definition: It refers to extending reality by some means, or using systems to augment or replace our perception of reality.
It is a spectrum where one end is the complete replacement of reality with virtual reality systems, and the other end is the complete replacement of virtuality with the entirely real world.

L02.subgoal: Identify key application domains and assess the market potential of extended reality

key_points.text: This lecture will cover different application areas and system categories pertaining to extended reality (VR and AR).
Extended reality technologies show huge potential across various application areas.
Key application areas include video games, healthcare, engineering, live events, and military.
Even small percentages of application areas, such as 4% in military, represent a significant financial amount.

L02.subgoal: Identify and describe major application domains of immersive technologies

key_points.text: Gaming and entertainment is a prominent application where users wear VR devices to experience immersion.
Healthcare uses immersive technologies for medical education and training, sometimes incorporating Mixed Reality (MR).
Education is an emerging domain that improves learner engagement and outcomes from primary to tertiary levels.
Travel and tourism utilizes virtual tours and digital heritage preservation to allow users to explore places remotely.
Defense applications include specialized military training and simulating combat environments in a virtual world.

key_terms.definition: VR technologies essentially refer to immersive technologies where our senses are blocked and we are transported to the virtual world.
Virtual tours are experiences that give the user the experience of visiting a place without physically going there.
Virtual tourism is a popular method that allows users to explore faraway places while saving money and physical effort.
Heritage tourism allows users to visit a heritage place virtually, enabling them to explore every part of the space without physically going there.

L02.subgoal: Compare and contrast non-immersive, semi-immersive, and fully immersive VR systems

key_points.text: VR systems are broadly categorized into three types: non-immersive, semi-immersive, and fully immersive.
Non-immersive VR provides a virtual experience through a computer where the environment does not directly interact with the user, often relying on standard displays.
Semi-immersive systems offer partial immersion by blocking only some sensory organs, such as when using a VR headset for virtual tours.
Fully immersive systems completely block the user's ability to sense the real world, replacing reality with virtual realism.

key_terms.definition: A virtual experience obtained through a computer where the user can control characters or activities within the software, but the environment is not directly interacting with the user.

L03.subgoal: Identify and describe diverse application domains and practical examples of Augmented Reality

key_points.text: Unlike VR, which emphasizes immersive experience, AR focuses on augmenting real-world content with digital content.
AR applications span various fields, including archaeology, architecture, industrial manufacturing, and commerce.
In commerce, AR enhances customer experience by allowing users to virtually test products, such as placing furniture in a room or trying on cosmetics.
In healthcare, AR supports diagnosis and treatment by providing real-time information, such as visualizing a patient's internal vein network.

key_terms.term: Augmentation of real-world content with digital content
key_terms.definition: This is the focus of AR, which involves adding digital content onto real-world content.
This is a term emphasized when discussing VR, but it is not mandatory in the case of AR.
This is an interesting application area where lost structures can be added to the screen using AR.
This is an augmented reality application that allows users to measure heights or lengths without needing a physical tape.
This refers to providing customers with the ability to test or visualize products in their environment before making a purchase decision.
This is an option that enables medical professionals to interact with patients using AR.

L03.subgoal: Differentiate between marker-based and markerless AR applications and their subcategories

key_points.text: AR applications are broadly categorized into two technological types: marker-based and markerless applications.
Marker-based AR uses physical markers, such as QR codes, to trigger digital content augmentation.
Markerless AR is more versatile, relying on computer vision techniques and not requiring physical markers.
Markerless AR has four subcategories: location-based, superimposition, projection-based, and outlining-based.

L03.subgoal: Compare and contrast the system categories and application focuses of VR and AR

key_points.text: VR systems are categorized based on psychological experience into non-immersive, semi-immersive, and fully immersive types.
AR systems are broadly categorized by technology into marker-based and markerless systems.
Marker-based systems are easy to create but require a sanitized environment, while markerless techniques primarily rely on computer vision.
VR emphasizes immersive applications, whereas AR focuses on augmenting digital content onto the real-world view.

key_terms.definition: These three categories (non-immersive, semi-immersive, and fully immersive) are based on the importance of the psychological aspect and user experience.
These systems are easier to make and rely on simple algorithms, but they are difficult to maintain unless the environment is highly sanitized.
These techniques are used to overcome marker maintenance issues and primarily rely on computer vision, sometimes utilizing other sensors.
